questions.question: Which of the following is one of the biggest challenges involving people's mind regarding transformation from existing system to the e-enabled system?

options.A: Financial concern
options.B: Security concern
options.C: E-Fear
options.D: Change resistance

questions.explanation: When people move from a familiar paper-based or manual system to a new electronic one, the most cited psychological barrier is an apprehension specifically about using electronic/digital tools themselves — often labelled 'E-Fear' in e-Governance change-management material — distinct from general organizational change resistance. Financial and security concerns are narrower, situational worries rather than the pervasive mindset barrier being asked about, and change resistance is the broader umbrella term, while the question points at the technology-specific fear driving that resistance.

questions.sub: Overview of approach for training in e-Governance projects
questions.question: How does "capacity building" contribute to the success of an e-Governance strategy?

options.A: By reducing the need for skilled professionals
options.B: By ensuring that government staff and citizens are trained and capable of utilizing new e-Governance systems effectively
options.C: By outsourcing all e-Governance initiatives
options.D: By focusing only on physical infrastructure development

questions.explanation: Capacity building succeeds by making sure the people who must actually operate and use the new system — both government staff and citizens — have the skills and confidence to do so, which directly determines whether an e-Governance rollout is adopted or abandoned. Reducing the need for skilled staff, outsourcing everything, or fixating only on physical infrastructure all work against, rather than support, successful adoption, since none of them build the human capability the strategy depends on.

questions.question: What is a key component of the people dimension of change that significantly impacts project success?

options.A: The number of new technologies introduced
options.B: Effective management of the people dimension
options.C: The cost of the new system
options.D: The duration of the project

questions.explanation: Change-management theory (and this syllabus's own unit on 'People dimension of change') holds that most e-Governance project failures trace back to inadequately managed human resistance, training gaps and communication failures — so 'effective management of the people dimension' itself is the key success factor. Technology count, system cost and project duration are project-management/technical variables, not people-dimension variables, so they do not answer what the question is specifically asking about.

questions.question: As far as knowledge is concerned, it has to be managed in the following series of steps — emerged, stored and ___.

options.A: Processed
options.B: Translated
options.C: Transcripted
options.D: Transferred

questions.explanation: The classic knowledge-management cycle is: knowledge is created/emerges, then it is captured and stored (in documents, databases, repositories), and finally it must be transferred/shared so others in the organisation can use it — closing the loop from individual to organisational knowledge. 'Processed' and 'Transcripted' describe handling of raw data, not the sharing stage of knowledge, and 'Translated' refers to language conversion, not knowledge dissemination.

questions.question:
Which principle of effective communication emphasizes that communication must be fully integrated with the change process?
(a) Communication is a one-time event.
(b) Communication should be done only at the beginning and end of the process.
(c) Communication should be handled by external consultants only.
(d) Communication must occur in parallel with the change process.

options.A: Communication is a one-time event.
options.B: Communication should be done only at the beginning and end of the process.
options.C: Communication should be handled by external consultants only.
options.D: Communication must occur in parallel with the change process.

questions.explanation: Effective change communication is continuous and runs alongside every phase of the change effort, not a single announcement — this is why option (d) is correct. Options (a) and (b) describe communication as an isolated or bookended event, which is precisely the mistake change-management best practice warns against. Option (c) is wrong because communication ownership should sit with project/change leadership working with stakeholders, not be outsourced entirely to consultants.

questions.sub: Key reasons for failures in change initiatives
questions.question:
Which of the following is a key reason for failure in a change initiative due to poor prioritization?
(a) All activities are given equal importance and taken up simultaneously.
(b) Customers' needs are thoroughly understood and incorporated.
(c) Employees are actively involved in the project.
(d) Clear benefits at the individual level are demonstrated.

options.A: All activities are given equal importance and taken up simultaneously.
options.B: Customers' needs are thoroughly understood and incorporated.
options.C: Employees are actively involved in the project.
options.D: Clear benefits at the individual level are demonstrated.

questions.explanation: Poor prioritization specifically means failing to rank activities by importance/urgency; treating every activity as equally important and attempting them all at once (option a) is the textbook symptom of that failure, spreading resources thin and causing overall project failure. Options (b), (c) and (d) all describe things done well (understanding customer needs, employee involvement, demonstrating benefits) and are recognised success factors, not failure causes, so they cannot answer a question asking for a 'reason for failure.'

questions.sub: Introduction and objectives of change management
questions.question: Many of the large organizations fade in time primarily due to —

options.A: Insufficient revenue generation
options.B: Insufficient capital
options.C: Lack in management
options.D: Non-adaptability to change

questions.explanation: A well-known observation in organisational and change-management theory (echoed by Darwin's 'it is not the strongest that survives but the most adaptable') is that large, once-dominant organisations decline chiefly because they fail to adapt to changing environments, technology and markets — not because of a single financial or managerial lapse. Insufficient revenue or capital (a, b) are symptoms that often follow non-adaptability, and 'lack in management' (c) is too vague/generic compared to the specific, syllabus-aligned concept of resistance to and failure of change.

questions.question: One of the primary challenges in management of change in transition to e-Governance is —

options.A: Technological change
options.B: Financial change
options.C: Manpower change
options.D: Leadership change

questions.explanation: e-Governance change management literature repeatedly stresses that the hardest part of transformation is not deploying new technology but retraining, redeploying and gaining acceptance from the existing workforce (manpower) whose roles, skills and daily processes must change — this is the 'people dimension of change' emphasised throughout the syllabus. Technological change (a) is usually the easier, more controllable part; financial change (b) and leadership change (d) are not the central challenges typically cited for e-Governance transitions specifically.

questions.question: When trying to classify change management into two types, what could be the most probable types?

options.A: Real change and superficial change
options.B: Incremental change and circular change
options.C: Radical change and transformational change
options.D: Incremental change and transformational change

questions.explanation: The standard two-way classification in change-management theory contrasts incremental change (small, continuous, evolutionary steps) with transformational change (large-scale, radical, fundamental shifts) — this genuine dichotomy is option (d). Option (c) pairs two near-synonyms ('radical' and 'transformational' both describe large-scale change) rather than a meaningful two-type split, so it is not a valid classification. Options (a) and (b) use non-standard, meaningless terminology ('superficial change', 'circular change') that does not appear in change-management theory.

questions.question: Which of the following provides the foundation for team development?

options.A: Motivation
options.B: Conflict management
options.C: Organizational development
options.D: Individual development

questions.explanation: Project management doctrine holds that individual development, both managerial and technical, is the foundation on which team development is built. Motivation and conflict management are practices applied within an already-forming team.

questions.sub: Introduction and objectives of change management
questions.question: The e-Governance change management affects –

options.A: Operational
options.B: Technological
options.C: The attitudes and behaviours of personnel
options.D: All of the above

questions.explanation: e-Governance change management is explicitly people, process and technology together: it alters operational routines, introduces new technology, and must shift the attitudes and behaviour of staff. Restricting it to any one dimension is the standard misconception.

questions.sub: Introduction and objectives of change management
questions.question: E-government implementation is complex due to the following reason:

options.A: Change Management
options.B: Design Management
options.C: Stake holder Management
options.D: Effort Estimation

questions.explanation: E-government projects are hard mainly because they change the way people work, so managing resistance, retraining and process re-engineering - change management - dominates the risk. Stakeholder management is part of that same problem, but change management is the umbrella term used in the NeGP capacity-building literature this question follows.

questions.question: Effective management of people dimension of change requires the following key goals:

options.A: Business Need,Design
options.B: Identify Obstacles, Reinforcement
options.C: Desire,Ability
options.D: Determine Implementation, Re-Engineering

questions.explanation: The people side of change is normally taught through the ADKAR model - Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement - and only option C gives two genuine ADKAR elements. Option B mixes one real element (Reinforcement) with 'identify obstacles', which is a project activity rather than a people-dimension goal.

questions.question:
Key Principles of Effective Communication.
Principle 1 : Organisational Change cannot occur without communication
Principle 2 : Communication is a single component of change process
Principle 3 : Communication planning applies to stakeholders, message delivery

options.A: Principle 1 is correct, Principle 2 & 3 are wrong
options.B: Principle 2 is correct, Principle 1 & 3 are wrong
options.C: Principle 3 is correct, Principle 1 & 2 are wrong
options.D: Principle 1,2,3 are correct

questions.explanation: Principles 1 and 3 are both plainly correct, which rules out options A, B and C, so the intended reading of Principle 2 must be the standard caution that communication is only one component of change management and cannot carry the change on its own. Awkward phrasing of Principle 2 makes this one read badly, but D is the only internally consistent choice.

questions.sub: Key reasons for failures in change initiatives
questions.question: Key reason for failure in change initiative may be:

options.A: There is continuity in the project team
options.B: The requirement of the customer is taken into account
options.C: Every activity is given equal importance and priority
options.D: Benefits at individual level are demonstrated

questions.explanation: Treating every activity as equally important means nothing is prioritised, effort is spread thin and the critical changes never get the attention they need - a well-known cause of change-programme failure. The other three options describe healthy conditions (team continuity, customer requirements captured, individual benefits shown) that support success rather than cause failure.

questions.question: Conduct Training Needs Analysis is an activity in what phase of change management approach?

options.A: Phase I : Establishing Foundation of Change
options.B: Phase II: Managing Change
options.C: Phase III: Sustaining Change
options.D: Phase IV: Verify Change

questions.explanation: Training needs analysis feeds the capacity-building and training rollout that happens once the change is actually being implemented, which is Phase II - Managing Change. Phase I is about readiness assessment, stakeholder identification and forming the change team, and Phase III is about reinforcement and institutionalisation.

questions.question: Change Readiness Survey is a tool which will:

options.A: Facilitate discussions involve change leaders
options.B: Identify key stakeholders
options.C: Measures the organizational readiness to change
options.D: Emphasize on exchange of information among a small number of participants through hands-on exercises

questions.explanation: A change readiness survey is a diagnostic instrument administered across the organisation precisely to gauge how prepared staff and structures are for the coming change. Identifying stakeholders and running hands-on workshops are separate change-management tools.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an internal factor driving change?

options.A: changes in human resources and skill levels
options.B: new management approaches
options.C: new product development
options.D: changes in local government elections

questions.explanation: Local government elections are part of the political environment surrounding an organisation, so they are an external driver of change. Human resources and skill levels, management approaches and new product development all originate inside the organisation.

questions.question: Why might workers resist change?

options.A: change could involve higher workloads
options.B: change could involve relocation
options.C: change could involve the breaking up of working groups
options.D: All of the above

questions.explanation: Resistance to change is driven by perceived personal cost - heavier workloads, forced relocation and the loss of established working groups and social ties are all standard causes listed in change-management literature. Since each option is a genuine cause, the combined choice is correct.

questions.question: What is the first stage in change management?

options.A: Sustaining change
options.B: Managing change
options.C: Establishing foundation for change
options.D: None of the above

questions.explanation: The standard three-phase change management approach used in e-governance capacity building runs Establishing the Foundation for Change, then Managing Change, then Sustaining Change. The first phase covers readiness assessment, stakeholder identification, sponsorship and forming the change team.

questions.question: Recognizing the need but on occasional basis, so that intensive innovation effort is followed by a period of inactivity refers to which of the following difficulties face by companies when they want to be innovative?

options.A: Failure of perception
options.B: Inappropriate innovation
options.C: Episodic innovation
options.D: Steady state innovation

questions.explanation: Episodic innovation is exactly the pattern described - innovation treated as an occasional burst of effort followed by a dormant period, rather than a continuous capability. Failure of perception means not recognising the need at all, and steady state innovation is the opposite problem of only improving what already exists.

questions.sub: Key principles for change management design
questions.question: A principle common to change management frameworks used on e-Governance programmes is that the change effort should be:

options.A: Initiated at the project conception stage and run in parallel with the technical implementation
options.B: Started only after user acceptance testing is signed off, so that the system being described is final
options.C: Delegated wholly to the implementation agency as one of its contractual deliverables
options.D: Confined to the department's IT cell, since it is the cell that will operate the new system

questions.explanation: Change management is designed alongside the solution because the process, role and structural changes it must prepare people for are decided during design, not at rollout. Waiting for UAT sign-off leaves no time to address resistance, and by then the redesigned workflows are already frozen.

questions.sub: Key principles for change management design
questions.question: Change management design principles insist on visible ownership by the senior-most administrative authority of the department rather than by the project manager alone. The main reason is that:

options.A: The sponsor is the officer who countersigns the implementation agency's invoices
options.B: Sponsors are expected to attend every user training session personally
options.C: Redesigned workflows alter roles and accountabilities that only the department's own authority can sanction
options.D: Financial rules require the senior-most officer to chair the technical evaluation committee

questions.explanation: An e-Governance project changes who does what and who is answerable for it, and those are departmental decisions no project manager can make stick. Invoice signing and tender committee roles are procurement duties, not the reason sponsorship matters to change acceptance.

questions.sub: Understanding scope of change in an e-Governance project
questions.question: An assessment of the scope of change in an e-Governance project that covers only the new application and the hardware to be deployed is regarded as incomplete because:

options.A: Computing hardware depreciates faster than application software does
options.B: Application licences normally have to be renewed every year
options.C: Users generally prefer manual registers to digital records
options.D: The project also changes work processes, job roles and often the departmental rules that govern them

questions.explanation: Scope of change is assessed across technology, process, people and the policy or procedural rules framing them; leaving out the last three understates what users are actually being asked to absorb. Licence renewal and depreciation are asset management concerns and say nothing about the extent of organisational change.

questions.sub: Understanding scope of change in an e-Governance project
questions.question: Digitising an existing manual form without altering the underlying procedure, approval chain or roles is best described as which magnitude of change, compared with a project that re-engineers the procedure itself?

options.A: Transformational change, because the medium of the record has changed
options.B: Incremental change, since the process logic and the roles remain as they were
options.C: Disruptive change, because staff must now learn new software
options.D: Structural change, because additional server capacity is introduced

questions.explanation: Magnitude of change is judged by how far process logic, roles and accountability shift, not by how new the technology feels. Learning a data entry screen is a training need; it does not by itself make the change transformational.

questions.sub: Identify enablers and disablers to change
questions.question: In a change readiness assessment for a department moving its services online, which of the following would normally be recorded as a disabler rather than an enabler?

options.A: A procedural rule that still requires a physical signature on the paper file before the case is closed
options.B: A budget line already sanctioned for capacity building activities
options.C: A department head who personally chairs the fortnightly project review
options.D: Staff who already use a departmental email system in their daily work

questions.explanation: A surviving requirement for wet-ink signature forces the office to keep running the paper process in parallel, which is the classic procedural disabler of an online workflow. Sanctioned training funds, active leadership review and existing digital habits all lower the cost of change and are enablers.

questions.sub: Identify enablers and disablers to change
questions.question: The chief practical purpose of separately listing enablers and disablers early in an e-Governance project is to:

options.A: Decide which of the shortlisted bidders should be awarded the implementation contract
options.B: Compute the liquidated damages that would become payable if the project is delayed
options.C: Allow a specific intervention to be planned against each disabler while existing enablers are deliberately leveraged, before rollout
options.D: Fix the number of servers to be provisioned in the state data centre

questions.explanation: The list is an input to the change plan: each disabler is matched to an owner and a countermeasure, and each enabler is used rather than left idle. Bidder selection, damages and sizing are procurement and technical decisions that the enabler-disabler analysis does not drive.

questions.question: Why is a change champion network for a state-wide e-Governance rollout usually drawn from staff spread across districts, offices and grades rather than constituted as a single team at headquarters?

options.A: Because headquarters staff are generally too senior to be sent for training
options.B: Because the implementation agency's contract prescribes a minimum headcount per district
options.C: Because a distributed team reduces the travelling allowance charged to the project
options.D: Because a peer in the same office and grade carries more credibility with users than a headquarters or vendor team does

questions.explanation: Acceptance travels through peer influence, so a champion who shares the users' office, grade and daily constraints is heard where an outside team is not. Travel cost and contractual headcount are incidental and would not by themselves justify the network structure.

questions.question: When a change champion network is being constituted, the most appropriate basis for selecting its members is:

options.A: Position in the departmental seniority list
options.B: Informal influence among colleagues combined with genuine willingness to support the change
options.C: Possession of a formal qualification in information technology
options.D: Physical proximity of the member's office to the project management unit

questions.explanation: Champions work through credibility and persuasion, so influence with peers and personal buy-in matter more than rank or technical credentials. Nominating by seniority tends to produce members who neither believe in the change nor have informal reach.

questions.question: Besides carrying project messages down to colleagues, the other essential function of a change champion in an e-Governance project is to:

options.A: Carry ground-level concerns, workarounds and sources of resistance back to the project team
options.B: Certify the implementation agency's payment milestones
options.C: Draft the technical specifications for the application modules
options.D: Conduct the statutory financial audit of the project accounts

questions.explanation: The champion role is a two-way channel: it is the upward flow of ground realities that lets the project team correct design and communication before resistance hardens. Payment certification, specification writing and audit belong to project management, technical and finance functions respectively.

questions.question: How does the role of a change champion differ from that of a departmental master trainer?

options.A: The champion delivers classroom sessions, while the master trainer only prepares the courseware
options.B: The champion is engaged by the implementation agency, while the master trainer is a departmental employee
options.C: The champion operates only during the pilot phase, while the master trainer operates only after go-live
options.D: The champion works on acceptance, motivation and sustained use, while the master trainer transfers specific operating skills

questions.explanation: A master trainer answers 'how do I do this', whereas a champion addresses 'why should I do this at all' and keeps the new way in use once training is over. Both are usually departmental staff and both operate across phases, so employer and timing do not separate the roles.

questions.question: A communications plan for an e-Governance rollout is considered adequate only when, for each identified stakeholder group, it specifies:

options.A: The number of press advertisements to be released in each district
options.B: The budget head from which publicity expenditure will be met
options.C: The message, the channel, the frequency and the person responsible, together with a defined route for feedback
options.D: The languages in which the application's user interface will be made available

questions.explanation: Communications management is stakeholder-wise planning of what is said, through what medium, how often, by whom, and how responses come back. Advertisement counts and budget heads are execution details, and interface language is a solution design decision.

questions.question: Change management practice recommends beginning communication early in an e-Governance project even when many implementation details are still unsettled, chiefly because:

options.A: Early communication is what discharges the department's proactive disclosure duty
options.B: In the absence of official information, staff fill the vacuum with rumour, which is far harder to correct later
options.C: It allows the tender for the implementation agency to be issued sooner
options.D: It reduces the number of training days that will eventually have to be funded

questions.explanation: Uncertainty about job security and workload generates speculation the moment a project becomes visible, and a correction issued after a rumour has settled costs far more effort than an early honest message. Disclosure obligations and tender timelines are unrelated to the timing logic of internal change communication.
